# What the letters mean {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}l c l l Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Quantity & Letter & Unit & Unit symbol & Simple meaning\\
\midrule
Current & $I$ & ampere & A & How much electric charge is moving.\\
Voltage & $V$ & volt & V & The electrical push across two points.\\
Resistance & $R$ & ohm & $\Omega$ & How strongly a part limits current.\\
Power & $P$ & watt & W & How quickly electrical energy is used.\\
Energy & $E$ & joule & J & The total amount of energy used.\\
Charge & $Q$ & coulomb & C & The amount of electric charge.\\
Time & $t$ & second & s & How long something happens.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\textbf{Why is current written as $I$?} $I$ means current. It comes from the older phrase \textit{current intensity}.
```

# Subscripts: the small letters and numbers {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l l Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Example & Read it as & Meaning\\
\midrule
$I_T$ & total current & Current for the whole circuit.\\
$I_1$ & current one & Current through part or branch 1.\\
$I_2$ & current two & Current through part or branch 2.\\
$V_S$ & source voltage & Voltage supplied by the source.\\
$V_{\mathrm{out}}$ & output voltage & Voltage measured at the output.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
```

# Significant figures {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}p{0.29\textwidth} Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Situation & What to do\\
\midrule
Multiply or divide & Use the fewest significant figures in the question.\\
Add or subtract & Use the fewest decimal places in the question.\\
During the calculation & Keep the full calculator value.\\
Final answer & Round once. Include the unit.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
```

# GUESS method {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries\large}c l Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Letter & Step & What to write\\
\midrule
G & Given & List the known symbols, values, and units in a table.\\
U & Unknown & List what you need to find and its unit.\\
E & Equation & Write the general equation, then rearrange it.\\
S & Substitute & Put the numbers and units into the equation.\\
S & Solve & Calculate, round once, include the unit, and write an answer sentence.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
```

```{=latex}
\newpage
\begin{center}
{\Large\bfseries\color{TEJNavy} Circuit Calculations}\par
{\normalsize Ohm's law, power, series circuits, and parallel circuits}
\end{center}

\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\textwidth}
\section*{Ohm's law}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Find & Formula & Units\\
\midrule
Voltage & $V=I\times R$ & volts (V)\\
Current & $\displaystyle I=\frac{V}{R}$ & amperes (A)\\
Resistance & $\displaystyle R=\frac{V}{I}$ & ohms ($\Omega$)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\textwidth}
\section*{Power and energy}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Use when you know & Formula & Unit\\
\midrule
Voltage and current & $P=V\times I$ & W\\
Current and resistance & $P=I^2\times R$ & W\\
Voltage and resistance & $\displaystyle P=\frac{V^2}{R}$ & W\\
Power and time & $E=P\times t$ & J\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
\end{minipage}

\textbf{Pick the equation that matches what you know.} Use $V$ for voltage, $I$ for current, $R$ for resistance, and $P$ for power.

\section*{Series circuits}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=black,boxrule=1pt,arc=0mm,left=2mm,right=2mm,top=1.5mm,bottom=1.5mm]
\centering\Large\bfseries\color{TEJNavy} ONE PATH. SAME CURRENT THROUGH EVERY PART.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{minipage}[c]{0.43\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{../schematics/bw/Series_Rule_Reference.pdf}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[c]{0.54\textwidth}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l >{\centering\arraybackslash}Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Quantity & Rule\\
\midrule
Current & $I_T=I_1=I_2=\cdots$\\
Voltage & $V_T=V_1+V_2+\cdots$\\
Resistance & $R_T=R_1+R_2+\cdots$\\
Power & $P_T=P_1+P_2+\cdots$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{minipage}

\textbf{Remember:} Same current everywhere. Add voltage drops, resistances, and load powers.

\section*{Parallel circuits}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=black,boxrule=1pt,arc=0mm,left=2mm,right=2mm,top=1.5mm,bottom=1.5mm]
\centering\Large\bfseries\color{TEJNavy} MORE THAN ONE PATH. SAME VOLTAGE ACROSS EVERY BRANCH.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{minipage}[c]{0.43\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{../schematics/bw/Parallel_Rule_Reference.pdf}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[c]{0.54\textwidth}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l >{\centering\arraybackslash}Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Quantity & Rule\\
\midrule
Voltage & $V_T=V_1=V_2=\cdots$\\
Current & $I_T=I_1+I_2+\cdots$\\
Resistance & $\dfrac{1}{R_T}=\dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\cdots$\\
Two resistors & $R_T=\dfrac{R_1\times R_2}{R_1+R_2}$\\
Power & $P_T=P_1+P_2+\cdots$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{minipage}

\textbf{Remember:} Same voltage on each branch. Add branch currents and powers. $R_T$ is smaller than the smallest branch resistance.

{\normalsize Use the prefix to replace a power of ten}

\begin{tejnote}[Capital letters matter]
$M$ means mega, but $m$ means milli. On the calculator, $1.0\mathrm{E}6$ means $1.0\times10^6$.
\end{tejnote}

\section*{Engineering notation examples}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l l l Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Original value & Engineering form & Prefix form & What changed\\
\midrule
$0.000\,047\ \mathrm{A}$ & $47\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{A}$ & $47\ \mu\mathrm{A}$ & $10^{-6}$ became micro.\\
$4700\ \Omega$ & $4.7\times10^3\ \Omega$ & $4.7\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ & $10^3$ became kilo.\\
$2\,200\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$ & $2.2\times10^6\ \mathrm{Hz}$ & $2.2\ \mathrm{MHz}$ & $10^6$ became mega.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
```
